I really enjoy the game, but some of the design choices are legitimately irritating. For example: 1. The game starts you with 5 masks, yet something that becomes quickly apparent is that many enemies and nearly every boss deals 2 masks of damage every time they hit you. This makes the first mask feel significantly less impactful to earn, since Hornet goes from dying in 3 hits to still dying in 3 hits. 2. Grinding is practically a requirement if you want to regularly use your tools or the architect crest. In general it feels like this game is significantly more willing to waste your time than the original was. 3. The runbacks are unnecessarily long. For one boss in particular the runback is longer than the boss fight itself. Team Cherry did an amazing job with the narrative and the environmental story telling was top notch. Many of the moments I find frustrating do a fantastic job at conveying the horrors of Pharloom. Nevertheless, from a gameplay perspective, they still feel bad.

I've played Battlefield since 1942. The current game isn't terrible, but it just doesn't feel like a Battlefield title. It feels more like Call of Duty—and I've put in plenty of hours on COD as well. The Conquest maps mostly feel small, with only one exception. We're missing the signature large-scale, dynamic events that made past games memorable. There's no blimp exploding, no battleship crashing onto an island, no skyscraper collapsing—just a crane you can knock over. It seems like Battlefield is trying to sit in a middle lane between traditional BF and COD gameplay, which might end up alienating fans of both. We’ll have to see how future updates shape the game, especially now that EA is in uncharted waters after being sold off.

It really is a shame what was once my favourite game series has turned into. In the beta and at launch Battlefield 6 actually seemed decent and I was optimistic they may have finally figured out how to make a good Battlefield again and while there are improvements over 2042 it is sadly still not enough. I was expecting to put 1000+ hours into this game as I have with most other Battlefields but after just nearly 300 hours I had to admit myself it just isn't fun at all. The netcode wasn't great at the start but somehow it has just gotten worse as time goes on. You can immediately tell if the netcode is ''on your side'' after your first gunfight in a match and sadly it is nearly always against you. Not that having it on your side really makes it any better as you can still clearly feel the unfairness. You can accept dying in what feels like one hit and having 0 time to react or dying when you are meters behind cover already if it just happens every now and then but it is nearly every game and has only become more unbearable since launch. One of the most important things in an online fps such as this is that it at least feels fair but this game just doesn't. The matchmaking is completely broken. Although they have never confirmed it my friends and I strongly suspect there is some sort of skill based matchmaking being used and I do believe this is why they refuse to add a server browser for official servers. Really what is the reason to not have a server browser other than if you want to force players into your matchmaking system? This again ties into the game just feeling unfair. I'm not the best player in the world but i'm no means the worst and have no problems getting into the top 5 of the scoreboard in a match but any sort of skill doesn't seem to matter when 95% of your matches are completely stacked against you. Sure you get the odd match where you're on the team that completely steamrolls the other but again there is no fun in that at all. The worst part is the extremely rare times you do get a match that is somewhat balanced and the netcode is okay the game is actually fun to play but this makes it all the more frustrating. There is a good game underneath all that but their stubbornness and inability to fix things means you rarely get to experience that. The content updates are also extremely disappointing. While I understand Battlefield is now a live service game 2 maps a season (that don't even release together) with 2 or 3 new guns is simply not enough and when they do things like release the little bird in season 2 it is blatantly obvious they are just holding things back to pad out seasons rather than making extra actual content. The battlepass is mostly filler too, what the game lacks in new maps and weapons there is no shortage of cosmetics and ''limited time modes'' which I guess is great if you're into that but most people aren't. I don't know a single person who would rather have another limited time mode that will be forgotten in a week over another map. The game already has the main Battlefield modes people buy it for with conquest, breakthrough, rush and a few smaller modes like TDM. Why do they insist on adding these things no one asks for? Portal seemed like it could be good until they yet again completely nerfed it immediately after launch. Personally i'm not someone who enjoys leaving my PC on in a portal server for hours to unlock everything but at the same time I really don't care if other people do. The game has 5000 ranks and while it doesn't seem fun if people want to just unlock all their weapons without actually engaging in pvp who cares? But the real downside to nerfing the xp in portal isn't that people can't boost its that it just automatically guarantees no one will use it. There has been some very interesting modes and maps people have created in portal that are completely dead because the simple fact is people still want to earn xp for playing and you can't do that if your server has any bots in it. They have also outright removed player created maps from other games (i.e shipment from call of duty). They provided a decent map editor that will just go to waste now. Why not have a monthly community vote or something on player created maps and add them into some sort of rotation or even turn them into actual maps? I saw several maps created from the California update alone that are all now completely dead. People are literally doing your job for you creating new maps and experiences but again they just seem to refuse to capitalise on any of it and it is so frustrating. I could go on but I think that gives you a good idea of where Battlefield is now. It used to be an amazing series that would take up nearly all of my time but the thought of playing it anymore is just tiring. The game will continue to haemorrhage players if they continue in this direction and sadly I don't see it changing. Look how many people have gone back to older Battlefield titles these past few days since they went on sale, you have the formula right there on how to make a Battlefield people want DICE so why do you refuse to do it?

The music in this game is absolutely outstanding—the combination of vocals, cello, violin, and piano creates a distinctly classical atmosphere. The tracks that left the deepest impression on me were Lumière and Alicia. Important story moments and boss battles are accompanied by corresponding OSTs, especially Une vie à t'aimer during the fight with Renoir. Speaking of Renoir, I absolutely love how his gentleman cane produces heavy, resonant sound effects with every strike against the ground—such an effective way to build tension and oppression. The presentation and camerawork are equally impressive, with masterful use of light and shadow, precise character eye contact and facial expressions, and even positioning all executed to perfection, plus wide-angle shots employed after battles conclude. Reading the final journal of Expedition 60, I felt profound sorrow—Lumière was right there before his eyes, yet he ultimately couldn't outswim the Gommage to bring the intel back to Lumière. At the very end of the game, I returned to where it all began and found the Picto Gustave had left for me. And I must mention—the choice at the ending branch was agonizingly difficult to make. Let us recall once more the musical fragments of Lumière and Alicia: Lumière: F5 F5 F5 E5 D5 F5 F5 F5 E5 D5 | F5 G5 F5 E5 | F5 F5 F5 E5 D5 F5 F5 F5 G5 F5 | E5 D5 E5 C5 Alicia: G4 + G5 C5 + E5 + G5 + C6 E5 + E6 | D5 + F5 + B5 + D6 E5 + E6 D5 + D6 | G4 + B4 + E5 +G5 B4 + B5 | C5 + E5 + A5 + C6 And speak once more: Tomorrow comes.

I'm not gonna comment on performance because you'll likely read more than enough about it in the reviews. All I'm gonna say is I have a pretty beefy rig myself and experienced some pretty bad drops in performance which isn't exactly ideal when the game looks fairly muddy when you start looking up close. That being said. I think what killed MH: Wilds the most for me was how trimmed down everything felt compared to previous titles. I'm not one for artificial difficulty but if I don't have at least some challenge, then parts of the game just feel boring. There's no researching monsters to identify more things about them to aid in hunts, there's no expeditions to stock on needed supplies for hunts, there's just nothing to add to the hunt other than breaking out a stick and whacking away at it. This might work for the people who want nothing other than a monster arena style game but I don't think those types dominate the franchise. Another glowing problem with the game is the absolutely boring level design, it's not even close to other games and those who say otherwise are straight up lying. Windward Plains is a wide and empty desert with very little visual variety, you have a small oasis, some caves, lots of wide open spaces, and just overall nothing else going on. Compare this to Wildspire Waste which has the same desert style areas and caves, but also a riverlands, an isolated swamp, some steppes, and more. On the surface they seem similar but it comes back down to how EMPTY the worldspaces of Wilds feel. You have the same issue with Scarlet Forest, Oilwell Basin, Iceshard Cliffs, and the Ruins of Wyveria. But what feels worse is that each respective map starts to feel small and more like a corridor than a map which is a stark contrast to the prior games which were either much more open or at least had more flow to them with intertwining paths. Not to mention a total lack of unique locales such as Coral Highlands or Rotten Vale. It took me a relatively short time to become bored of the world it was making me inhabit. I hope the expansion truly breathes some life back in the game but I honestly don't have much faith that they will. What a monumental fumble of what could've been a title that surpassed everything before it.

I came here to live A lot has changed between the time I played the first game and the second. Funnily enough, given the setting, in the meantime, I got into historical reenactment, larp and fencing. I became a bit of a handcrafter, a bit of a historian, and a bit of a swordsman Naturally, I approached KCD2 with a much more critical eye than I did the first game. Honestly, I never even considered the KCD a masterpiece, so the sequel didn't exactly have an enormous amount of goodwill to burn through. KCD was solid, sure, but it never lived up to the “second Witcher” hype people kept throwing around at the time. And then KCD2 somehow became that game. It completely surprised me and made me fall for it hard, even though I was looking at it with way more skepticism. Once you get invested in the story, it doesn't let go until the very end. This is storytelling in the truest sense of the word. Not just some excuse for the protagonist to exist in an open world, as is the case with so many games, but one coherent, genuinely compelling story. It has fantastic twists, memorable characters, moments that are both heartbreaking and hilarious, and dialogue that rarely lets you get bored. Every second or third cutscene had me going "♥♥♥, how the hell did they pull that off? These absolute madmen" Taking this story in felt as good as it must have felt for the developers to make it. This is genuine art. It's not another game that sucks the life out of you in exchange for a hundred pointless activities. This thing was made with love, and it lets you feel as though you're living another life. And that "another life" thing applies to the characters too. You can feel that the actors weren’t just playing these roles, they were living them I randomly stumbled across videos and streams featuring Tom McKay (Henry) and/or Luke Dale (Hans), and ♥♥♥, these guys seem to live and breathe this game even outside of work. Luke Dale genuinely seems to identify with the character he played, even in real life. That's an incredible level of commitment to a role. That kind of dedication is rare, and from what I can tell it was shared by a huge part of the development team and cast. That’s what makes this world feel alive. The more you dig into the people behind the game and watch stuff about the development process, the more you realize just how much love and soul went into it. That said, it wasn’t all smooth sailing. The game still has bugs and some unbalanced, poorly thought-out moments, although far fewer than the first one. Combat is still far from perfect. What really pisses me off is the continued existence of "ice skating" - when your positions sync up for animations. If an opponent parries your attack from a distance, he’ll just slide toward you like he’s on ice so the animation can play out. It completely kills any sense of weapon range. Polearms especially feel pointless; a guy with a short mace or sword will just skate right up into your face so he can ignore the reach advantage your longsword or a spear is supposed to give you. From my own time spent fencing, I’ve learned that not only the length of your sword, but even your height and the length of your arms actually matter in a fight - but none of that matters in the game. On top of that, Henry constantly gets stuck on branches and rocks in fights, his movement becomes sluggish, and since you can’t look down at your feet during combat, it gets really annoying - especially when you’re trying to backpedal while fighting ten guys at once. Some quests are needlessly, almost sadistically convoluted. It doesn't happen too often but sometimes you’ll get something like: "Find Zbysek. Last person who saw him was Jesek. Jesek has disappeared, so go talk to Pasek. None of them will tell you anything until you talk to ♥♥♥, and ♥♥♥ first. They're all in different towns, so enjoy running around the map talking to fifteen different people who have nothing more interesting to say. Congratulations, you've finally found Zbyshek." It was annoying, but truth be told, there are only a handful of quests like that. And that’s pretty much the entire list of real complaints. For a modern AAA game, that’s a short list. It’s a price I’m more than willing to pay for the immersion this game delivers. The game is worth almost every single hour you put into it. In the end, I din't play this game. I lived here Because even when you're not following the gripping main story or doing interesting quests, Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is one of the best immersive sims out there. When you boot it up, you won't be thinking "I’ll just knock out a couple of quests" or, worse, "I’ll clear a few outposts and do some dailies" You will be thinking "I’m going in there to live" Because ♥♥♥, you really do live in this game. I don’t know how these absolute maniacs pulled it off, but sometimes it’s pure joy just walking through a medieval town, stumbling into random events, taking part in this life, competing in tournaments, walking into any house and looking at how people live, then riding out into the fields, finding a pasture full of cows and going up to each one going "hello, cow" chasing around ridiculous squealing little piglets, or just looking at the beautiful horses. The only thing missing is the ability to set up camp like in RDR2. And a special mention goes to the blacksmithing. As someone who genuinely appreciates the craft, I spent a ridiculous amount of time in this game just forging things. That's the magic of it. There's always something to do, but you don't always need a quest marker telling you what it is. Sometimes you just want to exist in this world for a while. That's ultimately the best thing I can say about Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2. It's a literal window into another world. It has a gripping story and a living, breathing environment that's a joy to immerse yourself in, even when you're doing absolutely nothing of importance. In the end, this game completely won me over. My appreciation for it is on an entirely different level. It's earned a place among my all-time favorite games. I'm genuinely happy I got to spend time in this world. And someday, I'll be back.

Well, as much as I hate to write this review, I can't recommend the game at its current state. To start off, the community is literally doomed, the game has lost around 90% of its player count. Now, how does that affect the game? Let me explain. You see, back when the game launched, there was a lot of hype and talk about Arc Raiders, because it was truly a special experience. As a player, you could never really know who you might run into: whether the person was a casual player who wanted to team up and uncover ARC's mysteries, or a die-hard PvP enjoyer. That uncertainty was one of the things that made Arc Raiders special in the first place. As time went on, the community got split up by something called "aggression-based matchmaking," a system designed to make sure players who seek PvE end up in "PvE lobbies," while players who seek PvP end up in "PVP lobbies." Because of that, you now basically have to "choose" a playstyle to reach your goals: want to do quests and farm ARC for workbenches or projects? Go be a PvE player. Want to take other players' loot and hunt them down for fun? Go be a PvP player. This system doesn't sound bad on paper, right? Every player gets a lobby that matches their playstyle. Well, not quite. Because the community got split into two separate sides, both sides ended up worse off, not better. I'm a mixed playstyle player myself, I enjoy both sides of the game, and honestly that's exactly why this split bothers me so much. Neither side feels fully rewarding right now. On the PvE side: progression feels painfully slow. New projects, the main thing that gives PvE players a real long-term goal, only show up once in a while. You can spend hours doing quests and grinding ARC kills, and still be left waiting for the next project to actually drop. It just doesn't feel like there's enough consistently to chase. And in my opinion, the rewards you actually get from those projects aren't that good either, I'm not the only one who thinks so, from what I've seen a good chunk of the community feels the same way about it. On top of that, the Expedition system kind of sucks too. The only reason it's even worth doing, in my opinion, is the 5 skill points, some extra stash space, and the repair percentage buff, the repair buff being my main reason honestly. Everything else about it barely feels worth the trouble. And what makes it worse is that once you start an Expedition, you can't skip it, you're locked in and have to keep starting over again and again, or your progress and buffs just reset. That's especially painful in the game's current state, where you're already short on reasons to keep playing in the first place. On the PvP side: things aren't much better. A huge chunk of the players you run into are using free kits, meaning there's barely any risk on their end while you're the one putting your actual loot on the line. On top of that, cheaters are still a real problem. To be fair to Embark, they have been trying to do something about it: they've been testing map conditions that affect free kit availability, and they rolled out Denuvo Anti-Cheat alongside their existing Easy Anti-Cheat and Anybrain ML-based detection to try to catch cheaters earlier. It's a step in the right direction, but from where I'm standing, it still isn't enough to fix how the PvP side actually feels to play. And then there's Stella Montis, the map everyone knows as the PvP map. For some reason, every time my friends and I decide to risk our good loot and queue into a Night Raid there, that's exactly when things go wrong. We get picked off by campers or cheaters, and to make it worse, there's no hatch key available to fall back on for a safer extraction. So if the fight goes bad, we're stuck fighting our way out through the front door with everyone else. And if we instead queue into a regular match to avoid that? It barely helps. Almost everyone we run into is still using free kits, and on top of that, the match itself frequently spawns us in dark, Night Raid-like conditions anyway, so we end up dealing with the same visibility problems either way. Now, I want to be clear about one thing: I don't want Embark to rush out updates just to fill the silence. Rushed content usually means more bugs and half-baked features, and that's not what I'm asking for. But there does need to be a little bit more happening between these long update windows. Right now it just feels like too much dead time where both sides of the community are left waiting, one side for content, the other for the game to actually feel fair. Until PvE gets more consistent things to work toward, and PvP actually deals with free kits and cheaters in a way that holds up, I can't recommend Arc Raiders in its current state.

TL:DR - I'm conflicted I've followed the game for some time, ever since I heard about the AI/reinforcement learning implemented for the ARC machines. I normally would not play an extraction shooter/looter, but reconsidered purchasing after I heard about ABMM (Agression Based Match-Making). The idea behind it is, that if you don't shoot at others you will be put in the lobbies with more friendly players. This is where problems start; it created a division within the community. Some people really like it, some despise it - and there is a group that even gambles this system. The so called by the community "rat players" would attack unsuspecting players just before extracting, either posing as friendly players or hiding in a corner. This results in you being shot from behind, with no counter play - dead before you can respond. While this seems fun for the first few hours, it gets old quickly. Responding to human threats, ah! Here's another problem - if you shoot back, your ABMM raises and you get put into mixed lobby of peaceful players and aggresive players. Continue to shoot back, and you will be put in kill-on-sight lobby. In the end I just don't shoot back and write off every 6-10th game as a random loss. Not fun. The PVP crowd would say, that this is a part of the game and you should "get better" in PVP as it is a part of the game. But to get better you have to start shooting back, which will put you in strict PVP lobbies you might hate. The PVE crowd would say, there is a need to split PVE and PVP lobby to prevent this behaviour. But this would result in almost no challenge after you learn how the ARC machines operate and pointless resource grind. I don't know what is the right option, I don't want to guess. I can just say that whatever it is currently it is not it. Which is a shame, because the game is really good otherwise - good graphics, really well optimized. The machines are really cool. Should you choose to buy it, at least now you know what it struggles with.

I really enjoyed ARC Raiders when I first started playing. The gameplay was fresh, the atmosphere was fantastic, and every raid felt exciting. It had me hooked for quite a while. Unfortunately, the more I played, the less I wanted to log in. PvP has become the focus of almost every encounter, making it feel like you can’t enjoy exploring or completing objectives without constantly being hunted. Instead of feeling tense and rewarding, it often just feels frustrating. The community hasn’t helped either. It’s incredibly difficult to find friendly or cooperative players. Most encounters end in kill-on-sight, and the overall experience feels much more toxic than enjoyable. There really isn't much on this game that I can say that hasn't been said already, with that being said I'm going to praise every single aspect of this game. Hollow Knight: Silksong is what every sequel should strive to be. It expands on quite literally every aspect of the original game in such unique and interesting ways that allows it to have its own identity while still having all the core aspects of what make Hollow Knight well, Hollow Knight. Take the tool system for instance. It's this games twist on the charm system from the original, separating them into three types. Red tools which are combative weapons to attack the enemy with, blue tools which help in combat with effects like a longer needle or extra healing, and yellow tools which are there to assist with exploration. It's such a simple change from the original system yet it adds new layers of depth with the builds you're able to make and massively changes how you play the game depending on what you equip. This game is absolutely massive too. Hollow Knight had 19 distinct areas to it, each and every one of them feeling distinct with their own unique identities, enemies, bosses, puzzle, and items to pick up. Silksong on the other hand has 32 UNIQUE AREAS. That's just the size though, every area is squirming with things to discover, secret rooms, relics, new tools, skills, it just goes on and on. Every area in the game feel so fleshed out with how much there is to do in each of them, and even the ones that might be lacking in content compared to the rest make up for it with their atmospheres and lore that makes them a treat to go through, especially on repeat playthroughs. And the music, oh my god, the music. Christopher Larkin absolutely hit the ball out of the park once again the soundtrack to this game is stunning. The music serves it purpose so well in this game. Amplifying the mood of an area or the intensity of a boss fight to perfect degrees. Speaking of bosses, the bosses in this game are a step up from the ones in Hollow Knight. After taking the time to fight every boss in both of these games again and again I cannont understate how much of an upgrade the bosses are in Silksong compared to Hollow Knight, and the ones in Hollow Knight aren't even remotely bad! The bosses in Silksong are just THAT good. Lace, Fourth Chorus, Moorwing, Widow, Last Judge, Phantom, Cogwork Dancers, Trobbio, Karmelita, the list just goes on and on there are maybe only 3 bosses in this entire game that I'd say aren't at the very least "good" which there are definitely more than 3 in Hollow Knight that I'd consider bad. I'd also like to add another perspective here that just to praise this game a little bit more. You see I've done quite a bit of speedrunning for this game, and while I didn't ever speedrun the original Hollow Knight I get the feeling that this game is even better for that purpose than the original. The movement in this game is some of the best in any game I've ever played, and it makes for such a clean, satisfying game to play through or speedrun if you're into that. Seriously, I'd highly recommend learning the any% speedrun of this game if you're even remotely interested. There is so much more on this game I could write about, and maybe I will in the future, but to wrap this all up... Hollow Knight: Silksong is a perfect sequel, and I'd never change a thing about it. 10/10 no questions asked

I put over 400 hours into Blue Protocol: Star Resonance, so I definitely got my money's worth in terms of playtime. I enjoyed the game for a while, but I can't honestly recommend it to anyone looking for an MMO they can invest in long-term. Let's start with the positives. The visuals are excellent. The anime art style is beautiful, and the character creator gives you plenty of options to make a character that feels unique. Fashion is also one of the game's biggest draws—but it comes with a major caveat. While there are a lot of great cosmetics, many of the best outfits are locked behind limited-time gacha banners. On top of that, the dye system is surprisingly restrictive. Several outfits, including collaborations like Monogatari and Fairy Tail, don't let you freely recolor every part of the costume, which makes customization feel far more limited than it should. Unfortunately, that's where most of my praise ends. The story is incredibly forgettable. It mostly feels like you're moving from one area to the next without much reason to care about what's happening. The biggest issue is the endgame. Once you reach it, you realize just how shallow the gameplay loop really is. Every day becomes the same routine: gather and craft until you run out of stamina, either stop playing or burn potions to keep gathering, run your daily boss run (Unstable fights which take around 20 seconds with an AI party), and farm bosses hoping for imagines drops so you can play. I spent 6 months doing the same boss everyday and only had 1 imagine drop. ( Don't even bother tanking unless you have Tempest Ogre. He feels mandatory) That's... pretty much it. There are weekly raids, but unless you're in an active guild, you'll either struggle to find a group or hope you get lucky with a decent PUG. Progression is also frustrating because many groups refuse to accept players unless they already have an absurdly high Ability Score. It's a classic case gatekeeping. I joined a few guilds that simply carried me through the harder content. While I appreciated the help, it also made progression feel hollow because I wasn't really earning anything. The dungeon design doesn't help either. Most seasons simply recycle the same few dungeons across three different difficulty levels. New dungeons are added each season, but they usually boil down to pulling as many enemies as possible, AoEing everything down, and then fighting a boss. Seasonal events aren't much better. Most are either AFK events or small minigames that lose their appeal after a handful of runs. Eventually, I realized I was logging in every single day just to complete my dailies without actually having fun. Then the next season would arrive, wipe most of my progression, and send me back to square one. Instead of feeling rewarded for my time, it felt like I was on a treadmill that never went anywhere. I haven't logged in for a few weeks now, and honestly, it's been a relief. I don't miss the daily checklist. This game has a fantastic foundation. The visuals, character customization, and overall presentation are genuinely good. But the repetitive endgame, seasonal resets, shallow progression, restrictive cosmetic systems, and overreliance on limited-time gacha keep it from reaching its potential. I don't regret the time I spent with it, but I can't recommend it unless you're simply looking for a casual anime MMO to play for a season or two without expecting much depth.

Review: Battlefield RedSec (DLC) I was extremely disappointed with Battlefield RedSec. Battlefield 6 was an absolutely amazing game. I bought it at full price and never regretted it. It delivered exactly what I expect from a Battlefield title: large-scale battles, strong team play, and the classic zone capture gameplay that defines the franchise. However, RedSec feels completely out of place. The Battle Royale mode simply does not work in a Battlefield environment. It feels forced, unnecessary, and disconnected from what makes Battlefield great. The gameplay looks unpolished and uninspired, and overall it just doesn’t feel like Battlefield at all. Instead of trying to imitate games like Warzone, the developers should stick to their classic large-scale, objective-based warfare formula. That’s what Battlefield players love and expect. Honestly, I would rather start playing Warzone again than continue playing RedSec. This DLC does not live up to the Battlefield name and feels like a step in the wrong direction for the series.

The first time I played the original Kingdom Come game way back when it launched. I love the world, simulation but the janky combat very quickly ended my run. Then I came back years later and last month I was able to finish it. I enjoyed it but equally had a frustrating time with it. With KCD 2, things are different. Sure the combat still carries the jank and there are situations the game throws at you which is frustrating, but only this time the good parts massively outweighted the bad parts. The combat is tweaked to be faster, a bit simpler. Against one on one, it works really well, but when the game throws you 3 or more enemies, it can be frustrating super fast. Luckily enemies sort of take their turns in attacking you, unlike KCD 1. One design decision they carried over which I am not a fan of at all is their save system. I lost almost 2 hours of gameplay in KCD 2 because of it. I am absolutely not a fan of their quite to save loading, sleep or drink specific item to save. This is an open world simulation driven game, so if the stars alaign, death can come hard and fast. I immediately installed the F5 save mod, cause with it I would not have continued. The game's story, characters are signficaintly better than the first game. This is where game truly shines above the original. I cared about the characters and the plot a lot more than I did in the first game. Well written with great cast of supporting characters. The open world also took a big step up. The regions feels much more handcrafted with more attention to detail and diversity than the first game. Every where feels unique, which the first game didd not have. Also the game's biggest town, Kuttenberg is one of the most impressive medieval cities I've ever seen, bustly with life with npc's having their own schedules. All these running on a very impressive performance thanks to their modified Cryengine. The world looks stunning, only the character models and their facial expressions looks dated. Where the first KCD felt like a 6-7/10 game depending on the day. This game is easily 8-9/10 game. Really enjoyed it. Warhorse Studios, please go away from this restrictive save system, thank you.

Upsides: - This is the most beginner friendly Monster Hunter game. All of the menus are also easily understandable and responsive (even though having like 5 submenus for everything is annoying at times). - Good roster. Only a few boring monsters and 1 terrible (Congalala). - Good environment, huge attention to detail. Iceshard Cliffs is the only area which I've found annoying to fight in - The story is fine. Nothing groundbreaking but entertaining enough. The final boss of the Low Rank quest line is very good. The kid character did not annoy me unlike some other players who foam at the mouth the moment his name is mentioned (I really do not get the problem). - After 3 Title Updates the endgame is very solid and the difficulty is there. The "star" system is confusing at first but not that hard to understand, the difficulty progression is solid with 6, 7, 8 and 9 star monsters. Downsides - Of course, performance. Even people with good PCs still struggle with this game because the release was rushed so the optimisation is poor. There have been updates improving it a little but the game still struggles. The devs promised to improve the performance on December 16th with the release of Title Update 4, I hope it will actually be substantial (improving the performance of your game almost 1 year after release is kinda crazy not gonna lie) - In my opinion, the game lacks art style. The previous games were a product of their time and that gave them a certain style, the way they look is memorable. In Wilds they just went with super realistic, I wish there was more to it than that. The monsters are gorgeous, perhaps the playable characters could've been more cartoon-y. - The amount of handholding during the story gets tiring. Multiple missions where you gotta ride on your mount and you cannot stray from the path (your character won't let you), it's all mostly on walking speed. It wasn't the worst thing in the world and it was probably done to show off how much work they've done on the environment but at some point you've just had enough. - More of a late game issue but I wish Artian weapons weren't in the game until like Title Update 3. For most weapons, they are the best option so the Rarity 8 weapons you can make out of the hardest monsters in the game are mostly useless. Yeah, of course I could just not interact with the system, but it would be stupid to deny their advantage. *Update*: The game has received its final update. So, after the update and the TU4 from December last year, I can confidently say: Monster Hunter Wilds is a good Monster Hunter game. It has a slow start, however, the endgame is rich with content and variety of monsters to fight. The difficulty is all there, Gogmazios is alright, Savage Omega is still one of the craziest fights, the new 10* monsters pose a great challenge while not being too much of a slog (except the ever-boring Uth Duna), Arch-Tempered Arkveld is Cinema. The TU4 Gogma weapons have introduced even more annoying rng but it is what it is I guess. The artstyle is still my main downside, focus mode feels very handhold-y, other than that I have no complaints. The performance issues were fixed (at least for me), the game runs great. I have genuinely enjoyed playing this game and cannot wait for what the DLC will have in store.

I love PEAK. I’ve played it since launch and always look forward to new maps, achievements, and mechanics. It's obvious how much time and effort "Team PEAK" has put into this game. The devs are very community-oriented, respond to player suggestions and improvements and fix minor bugs and errors within a few days. I haven't seen any bug that negatively affected the gameplay which hasn't already been removed, except the well-known backpack glitch. Backpacks ragdolling under the map as soon as we put 'em down. Very rare, but still happens. (Mostly in the tomb, when the entrance is nearly fully covered by sandstone and you're putting down a backpack to get past a little hole, you got a huge chance you'll never see that lil baggy again. Since the tomb is optional, not that dramatic, but still room for improvement.) Another thing I'd love to see is the ability to create lobbies larger than four players without the need for mods. I personally love to use mods in general, but since PEAK is also a very family-friendly game and many people don't like using mods, I'd like to see the option to create bigger lobbies without them. Especially because we all know that new game updates + old mod versions aren't the best friends, and PEAK literally gets updated nearly every week. All in all, PEAK is an incredibly funny game and I can highly recommend it to anyone who's searching for a quirky alternation with friends and randoms, or an adventurous, almost meditative single-player experience. Not to unmention the various ascents (difficulties). They force you to try different packing methods, adapt your typical climbing tactics, use new paths to reach the peak, and in the end, get another cool cosmetic as reward for each ascent, which also definitely increases the replayability. No matter if you just wanna reach the Peak a few times with your friends, or go all in for achievement hunting and the full adventure trip, it's worth the price with or without a discount.

It certainly has a unique art direction, experimental storytelling, and it captures the spirit of digital nostalgia. While I would like to recommend this game to practically anyone, it's a matter of taste and personal preference, I can't in good faith tell anyone to play a live service Gacha Game. While the Sekiro inspired combat and Wuxia elements are fantastic, the underdeveloped MMO aspect of the game will likely wear a lot of players down over time. Three month long seasons, weak battlepass offerings, month-long stretches of time with nothing to do made up of time gated, drip fed, and buggy content that largely is comprised of mini games and weekly/daily runs of the same thing. Nearly every resource or incremental point of progress you make towards unlocking a free cosmetic/accessory is capped out. The resource farming is capped daily, coins are capped, everyday drops from monsters, crafting. I don't think there is a single system that doesn't have an internal limit to progression, even if it has no direct impact on PVE or PVP combat. I think the biggest killer of this title, for me, is the fact you run out of engaging solo content pretty early on, so you resort to trying PVP, Raids, and Abyss challenges. The raids can only be completed once per week, PVP is laggy and inconsistent (filled with bots), and the abyss trials are a fun challenge with little to no reward. Worst of all, outside of drip fed, time gated, energy capped content, is the abysmal integration of the Gacha system and no end-game trading system. I do appreciate it isn't explicitly pay-to-win, but the fact that it is so disconnected from the main gameplay loop makes it feel tacked on. Once again, you're capped to purchasing 3 premium pulls a week without forking over hundreds of dollars to get a single skin. The shop skins are 3x the price of CN servers, the Gacha is also wildly over priced (30 dollars for a single 10 pull btw) and a hard pity set at 150 which means virtually nothing. Hard pity doesn't guarantee the outfit, hitting hard pity then hitting pity again doesn't guarantee the banner reward. You have to spend on average around 400 dollars for a single item and there is no other way to purchase the premium currency without spending your college fund and selling your kidney. Here's my advice, play Sekiro, or Elden ring, Dark souls, or an actual MMO if you're into that. While I appreciate some of the potential depth of combat and the aesthetics, don't play aggressively monetized live service games like this. The lack of content, end game systems, and repetitive boring grind isn't worth it when the chance to get something good is less than .014% and the free outfits pale in comparison and take months to grind for (only because of hard caps.) I'll still revisit this game from time to time, and am willing to change my mind if the developers adapt, but I don't see that happening considering we aren't the main player-base. Until then, I'll be treating this game as if it's in maintenance mode for the next couple months (at least until Hengdao comes out.)

500 hours in Where Winds Meet and I’m still locked in—but I really need to talk about the translation and historical context. The game is gorgeous, the wuxia vibe is strong, and the combat still makes me feel like a martial arts legend (right before I get folded by some random NPC named “Hungry Bandit #3”). But the English translation definitely needs work. A lot of dialogue feels awkward or unclear, and important story moments sometimes lose impact because the wording just doesn’t hit right. The historical references are also interesting but under-explained. For example, when the game touches on regions like the Hexi Region, it clearly expects you to already understand the significance—but for most players, there’s not enough in-game context to connect the dots. I’ve had to pause multiple times just to look up what was actually being referenced. If the devs improve translation quality and add better historical grounding, this game goes from amazing to truly unforgettable. Still 10/10 experience—but I’m basically playing Where Winds Meet + Wikipedia simulator at this point.

Absolutely fantastic, underrated game. It's Entirely F2P friendly, not a single cent spent provides any sort of power or upgrades that cannot be earned within a VERY reasonable time through just playing the game casually. I'll tell you up front. Ignore the complainers that hover around the game. Sadly, and this is true of so, so, SO many facets of media these days, there are people who will bash anything and everything. According to the internet, 90% of videogame developers are idiots who don't know how to program games and "Waste potential" because they don't make the game EXACTLY the way each individual person wants. You can ask 10 different people and get 10 different answers as to "Why the game is failing" Meanwhile, it's the best performing Mecha game on the market right now, and a completely unique game in it's own right. Games like Cosmic Break and Starward play more like a fighting game in their way. Slower, more "frame data" centric style stuff. Mecha break will obviously pull comparisons to Armored core 6, but the main difference between Mecha break and Armored core is a big one: Mecha break is faster paced, and doesn't rely on you grinding for days or longer to unlock "the good parts" that you can actually use to play online, nor does it suffer from AC6's biggest flaw, the stamina system. No, not the ENERGY system. The stamina-break system. The stamina break system limited AC6 in SO many ways, and while it's absolutely possible to have a few fun rounds with friends using meme parts, if you go into any form of quickplay, you'll run into legions of the same minmaxed AC's. Mecha break snaps that in half by making each mech it's own unique hero, more akin to something like overwatch or titanfall, where it plays more like a hero shooter, with each Mecha (called strikers) having a unique, interesting kit that stands them apart from the rest. But what this does is encourage players to pick something that suits their sensibilities and playstyle, but offers a few variants on that style, usually by weight class. The game features a PLETHORA of modes, and by this time tomorrow as of the time of posting this review, we'll also have a co-op roguelike mode. So you have: • 6v6, Ranked and Unranked. • 3v3, Ranked and Unranked. • 1~3 player PVE co-op Roguelike modes. • 1~3 player extraction-shooter style modes, as well as a 1~3 Co-op PVE variant where the AI is more dangerous. • A 12 player free-for-all mode. Oh and from time to time they also run events that include things like co-op boss raids. So you have A PLETHORA of modes that allow you to pick what you're in the mood for, PVP or PVE, and you could absolutely play the game entirely in one mode or the other if that's all you want, or mix-and-match across the gamut to maximize your rewards and boost your credits up faster. If you're even REMOTELY competent, you can scrounge up the credits you need to unlock one of the handful of locked strikers in a few hours. You do have the option to skip the "wait" but it's barely a wait, honestly. There's paid games out there that make you grind more for unlocks and not by a little. This game is GENEROUS, with a striker unlock having a cost of 15'000, and each individual game you play averaging around 300~600 depending on your performance, and if double-credit weekend bonuses are going, and each mission gives you an extra 1000 which you can do 6 of a week. So if you do your weeklies, by the time you finish those, you'll EASILY have enough for a new Striker every single week and that's assuming you're taking your time. In the time I've been playing, I've already got 4 of them. OH AND THEY GIVE YOU A FREE TRIAL OF ONE OF THE LOCKED STRIKERS EVERY WEEK FOR YOU TO PLAY AND EVEN IF YOU OWN THEM ALREADY, YOU CAN DO BONUS MISSIONS WITH THEM FOR EVEN **MORE** free credits. You can easily, if you play consistently and diligently, milking every single credit out of the game you can, get every single locked striker for free in a month. That's nothing to sneeze at when it comes to free to play games. That's damn near UNHEARD OF in my 30 years of playing MMO's and F2P games. And with movement smoother than silk, Combat that naturally flows, and the unique customization systems such as having skins drop from just playing the game for free (In large numbers, mind you) and each one being unique even in it's own type? IE: If you have "Jungle stripe" and I have "Jungle stripe", our two camos might be completely different colors, in different positions, with different logos, but share the same "design" overall. It's actually REALLY unique and means no two strikers ever look IDENTICAL unless they explicitly try to. You'd have to be dead inside not to find something to love here.

Kingdom Come Deliverance II is one of those rare RPGs that feels less like a game world and more like a time machine. From the very moment you step back into late Medieval Bohemia, the game’s commitment to the historical time period is obvious. Landscapes and towns are modeled on real locations, armour is modeled from surviving musuem pieces of that era, Peasents/nobles in towns have daily routines mapped out, heck even the night sky has been modeled to be somewhat accurate to early 1400 Bohemia. This is not absolute however, balancing historical accuracy with enjoyability is always a tricky affair, and unless you are in the minority and you are a hard core history buff some things always get sacrificed to make the game enjoyable for all. It could be major things like there not being any children in the game at all, or smaller things like carrots anachronistically being orange. Where the dev's focused their efforts on being historically accurate they did so with spades. It’s this obsessive attention to detail that gives the game its immersibility. Getting back into the saddle with Henry is as punishing at times as it is rewarding. The combat is deliberate and skill-based like the first game. Positioning, stamina, and timing matter. Do things right and you feel like you can cleave your way through an entire army, but miss the parry or allow yourself to get riposted and you find yourself getting sent straight back to the load screen. The continuation of Henry's story feels natural and is very well written. The game excels at making large-scale events feel personal. You’re not saving the world you’re trying to survive and find your place in it. Choices matter and the story is filled morally ambiguous choices for the player to make, and they rarely feel simple or clean. The two regions are a big step up from the first game, The regions are overall quiet and beautiful to traverse, the notable fortresses are very well detailed internally as well as externelly but these pail in comparison to the standout location Kuttenberg. A bustling silver-mining city and economic hub, packed with shops, guilds, quests, and citizens which make the city feel dense and alive. These elements come together to make Kuttenberg arguably one of the most detailed cities ever built in an RPG. Overall, KCD2 to me isn't just a sequel, it’s a refinement of a very specific vision. A grounded, historically rooted RPG that prioritizes immersion. One that if you’re willing to embrace, it will offer you one of the most authentic RPG experiences ever created. 10/10

My early journey in this beautifully chaotic game: I began by sculpting a character so disturbingly misshapen that any divine being would request a refund, then immediately had to watch my monstrosity share screen time with flawless, idol-tier NPCs. Witnessed a bear attempting a mystical t’ai chi routine to nab a beehive, learned the same move, punted the bear into orbit, nearly died from bees and bruises, accidentally stole a horse, and got my skull rattled by its furious owner — leaving me with a collection of painful injuries. Out of nowhere, a stranger with a Chinese username — essentially Asian John Wick — joined my world, purged my ailments with a chakra battle straight out of a shonen anime, then politely asked to duel and proceeded to fold me like laundry before bowing and disappearing. Spiritually defeated, I swore to train as a healer, unlocked basic poison remedies, and practiced on a wounded goose because I wasn’t competent enough to treat actual players. Started experimenting on my guildmates with the chakra healing mechanic, slowly building expertise until I could mend everything from fractures to full-blown emotional collapse. Took on healing requests from random adventurers, entered their sessions, cured them, challenged them to honorable combat, and vanished like a wandering sage. Eventually reached such absurd medical proficiency that I could bypass the mini-game entirely and instantly fix even the nastiest conditions — still insisting on duels afterward out of ritual. Climbed to the top of the healer leaderboard, gained the nickname “the green-faced dueling physician” in world chat, and began receiving requests at a constant, almost comical pace. After more than a hundred successful healings — and zero duel losses — I got a message for a level 4 Soul Bind, one of the hardest afflictions in the game. The sender? Asian John Wick. I cured him once more, we clashed in an incredibly tight duel, I survived with literally 1 HP, and he knelt, offered a deep, respectful bow, said “GG,” and departed — confirming that I had officially become the game’s supreme healer.

As a huge Monster Hunter fan for a long time, I understand all of the criticism coming for the game, but I want to break it down into a handful of points. So if you don't mind a moment of your time, I would love to give an extensive review on the game after many many hours, and having played the beta, and been at one of the events showcasing the game to be playable to the public before release. 1. "It's too easy" Something I find with a lot of people when it comes to MH they play a souls-like and expect Monhun to be the same. I know this isn't everyone and I'll get into that, but first I wanna say that Monhun is a Monster Hunting game, I know shocker but that's why the game doesn't feel like some story of these over the top proportions. The lore and game is all about living with monsters and the balance of it all so applying a souls-like onto it doesn't work. On the other hand, for those who just say it's too easy, stop referencing Wilds to World, one of the biggest things in the community is saying "World is better and harder, Wilds is too easy" and truth be told, right now, it is. Because subconsciously you're relating G rank/Master rank to Low and High Rank. World had the exact same "issue" at launch for vets of the series, it's just what happens when you get good at a game comparing the skill ceiling between two games, even if in the same series is hard if you've played one before the other. I can say World is easy because I play MHG from time to time, or I could go back and play MH Tri and say it's too hard, but a Tri player could play World and say it's too easy. It's not about your skilllevel, it's about the overall level that is comfortable for casual and hardcore players. If you want a challenge, enjoy the challenge quests, or do the arch-tempered quests or fight Savage Omega. 2. Lack of Content Jumping off of my final point on the last part, lack of content is really overstated. For all games not just Wilds. If you look at any new release now, people are BEGGING devs for content updates almost all the time. I've seen it with this community where they release a huge update and instead of enjoying it and being happy, they request more. I understand it's a large company with lots of people, but the entire company is not working on that game, a small portion of the company is working on wilds still. "well just put more people on" -you can't exactly do that when whole entire games and systems need to be made. It's a lot for a team to concept, dev, texture, everything for an update. World had just about the same time for these content updates, but now people are so pushy for things here and now to get it over with and done. This gives the game more time to breath and allow newcomers to come in and not feel overloaded, I think that's what people are forgetting. 3. Performance I understand the issues people are having, and I get it, but i can also say I have been able to run MH Wilds on a laptop for months now just fine. It's not a gaming laptop, it's not some custom-built model, it's a Lenovo Thinkpad. My pc which is damn near 6-8 years old and about $1000 can run wilds on high just fine with a hiccup now and then when loading zones. A game of this size, with so many well-crafted zones and thought put into every nook and cranny is bound to be powerful like this and hard to optimize. I've talked to people who want to get into game dev who have said they have no idea how Capcom has even been able to optimize so far. If you really believe games like these, of this scale aren't going to be optimization hells at launch you're mistaken. A company can't make it optimized for every single person out there because they don't know every single person's setups, so they have to try everything and see what does and doesn't work. They need player feedback, not hostile player feedback, not kind, professional feedback. So I want to close this off by saying if you really aren't enjoying the game in its current state, take a break from it and come back. I adore this game and want to play 100s of more hours, I really do and I know I can. But I also know I want to take breaks as well to keep the spender of the game in my mind. It's such a beautiful game and not once have I felt taken out of the experience, sure when I first load in, one or two things may be polygonal, but that's also cause my GPU is old, but once it all loads in I'm right back into the immersive world that has been crafted and I've been allowed to venture into and enjoy. If you're getting tired of the difficulty of monsters, take a stroll and do some fishing or just watching the monsters and endemic life interact. That's not just a fun detail, it's apart of the game's experience, it's built for Monster Hunter. If you die and spawn at a camp, follow the palico that heals you, if you do, they run all the way back to the base camp of that area, best seen in Windward Plains. Amistrigian have an entire life cycle, Gelidron switch from oil to land to sunbathe and moisturize, the list goes on. Monster Hunter Wilds, and for the series in general has never been so alive than before in Wilds. It's not just about hunting the monsters or killing the boss, it's about those little moments in life that you would usually miss if you weren't looking hard enough. It's a great representation of nature and life itself, and looking past that and only staring at the flaws of the game is going to ruin the experience. I understand if its hard to see because of performance, but don't forget these are real people working on this game who have passion and love for this game just like you do. If they didn't they wouldn't be working on it in the first place. With that, a send off, Happy Hunting to all!

Gemini said Review: Kingdom Come: Deliverance II – A Beautiful, Tedious Mess If the goal of Kingdom Come: Deliverance II was to make me feel the crushing weight of 15th-century peasant life, then it is a resounding success. However, if the goal was to provide an engaging, functional gaming experience, it stumbles into the mud and stays there. Ambition Over Execution Developer Warhorse Studios clearly doubled down on the "hardcore realism" that defined the first game. While the scope of Bohemia is breathtaking, the performance is abysmal. Even on high-end hardware, the frame rate chugs in dense urban areas like Kuttenberg, and the pop-in is so aggressive it feels like the textures are being delivered by a medieval courier who keeps getting lost. Clunky Combat and Artificial Difficulty The directional combat system remains a polarizing nightmare. What is marketed as "skill-based" feels more like wrestling with a shopping cart in a hurricane. Henry’s movements are agonizingly sluggish, and the lock-on system is a death sentence when facing more than one opponent. The game mistakes tedium for depth; having to manage every minute detail of hygiene, hunger, and sleep doesn't add immersion—it adds chores. I spent more time looking for a bathhouse to wash off bloodstains so NPCs wouldn't scream at me than I did actually enjoying the narrative. Buggy Bohemia Then there are the bugs. From quest-breaking NPC pathfinding to physics engine freak-outs that launch Henry into the stratosphere, the game feels undercooked. It is frustrating to lose an hour of progress because your horse clipped into a fence and the "save-anywhere" feature is still tied to a limited in-game item. Final Verdict The writing and historical authenticity are top-tier, but they are buried under a mountain of technical instability and archaic design choices. KCD2 feels like a game built for a very specific type of masochist. If you enjoy fighting the controls as much as you enjoy fighting bandits, you’ll love it. For everyone else, this is a beautiful, bloated, and deeply frustrating experience that desperately needed another six months in the oven. Score: 4/10

This review contains no direct spoilers. It's nearly impossible for me to say why I don't like E33's story while being vague, but I'll try. "I'm not angry, just disappointed." A quote from a character in E33 which happens to describe how I feel about the game. Giving a negative review to a game that many consider "life-changing" and a "masterpiece" will probably make me seem contrarian for the sake of it. However, given the direction the story went and some of the more atrocious dialogue, I think E33 earned it, which is a shame because I thought for sure I'd love it. If you're thinking about buying it, I'd say be at least a little skeptical of the hype and consider whether or not the dialogue, the game's final act, and the ending all being "bad" could ruin the game for you before you do. If you expect a journey from E33, you'll probably get one, but a journey is remembered less fondly when the destination turns out to be ♥♥♥. Starting with the obvious positives, E33 is extremely cinematic and well-presented, the environments are stunning, and the music is amazing. Given these things, it isn't hard to see why someone would call E33 a genuine masterpiece. That said, I think this game deserves more criticism than it gets, particularly story/writing-wise. The boss Sirene feels like an unintentional representation of the game itself and how people feel about it (iykyk), and given the praise this game gets, I've had to ask myself whether or not I played the same one as everyone else. The gameplay of E33 should technically also be a positive since I do like it, but I do have to critique it a bit. Combat has a central focus on parries. This in mind, you'd think parrying would be rewarding, but it really isn't. If you parry all 7 hits of a combo string, what do you get besides AP you can easily get anyway? You get a single counter. And if you miss a single one of your parries, you are denied this small luxury. And because Elden Ring and its consequences have been a complete disaster for the human race, the developers looked at that game and really admired how many obnoxiously delayed attacks were in it and copied some homework. Have fun waiting a full 5 seconds for that one attack to land only for it to come out instantly on the 6th second. So while I like the combat on paper, and most of the time in practice, it does walk a line between being satisfying and being annoying. The dialogue in this game is usually good/fine, but weighed down by Marvel-esque quips and forced humor. You'll eventually hear characters use modern speech patterns and slang (I ♥♥♥ you not one of the characters says "Bromantic" + another moment where someone says "So which one is it?" only for another character to respond "Yes" in that funny internet way) to be "funny" and "lighten the mood." It's like the writers were told "make these characters feel real" and then they decided "characters feeling real" must equal "talks like a modern day person," which definitely doesn't break the tone or take you out of the setting or anything. The multiple palm prints on my face are the result of humorous dialogue, I assure you. Humor has its place in a dark story and I don't dispute that fact. The problem with E33's "humor" is that it's so desperate to be funny that it constantly breaks the tone of the story and doesn't care that it does. It irked me to the point where I legitimately did begin to care less about the story/characters after one too many forced attempts at a laugh. Some of these moments land and feel like they have a place, but the vast majority don't. Hell, even a few of the expedition journals you can find about people who died are played off as jokes, and when you compare those journals to the intro of the game, you'll probably just narrow your eyes or cringe if anything. Now for the story, as spoiler-free as possible: You're introduced to the world with some good hooks, but sadly this game peaks at its intro and goes steadily downhill. Things are fine for a time until act 1's finale, during which some events take place seemingly just for cheap shock value (plus characters acting stupid for the sake of the plot) and fail to justify themselves any other way. Actually, it isn't even that shocking - odds are you'll be able to predict what happens long before it does, so it doesn't justify itself that way either. The events aren't "bad" in the moment, but looking back later in the game, you realize they happened for no reason other than to set the stage for a ♥♥♥ plot twist. In the context of where the game goes, act 1's finale is garbage. It feels like someone said "Hey wouldn't it be cool/funny/random/shocking if we did this at this moment in the game?" and everyone just unanimously decided to throw it in for how quirky of an idea it was. Act 2's finale is even worse and tries too hard to pull off an M Night Shyamalan twist to the point where it just feels super jarring and random. Think of the dumbest, most random plot twist a story can have and there's decent odds you just guessed THE major plot twist of E33, or close enough to it that I wouldn't be able to say you were wrong. Act 2's finale pulls the rug out from under you so it can say "Ha, gotcha!", then takes the story in a bizarre direction and proceeds to hide behind annoyingly contrived twists. And despite the fact that these events are the storytelling equivalent of upending a set table for fun, you're still expected to care about what happens next and participate in like 60 hours of sidequest hell to provide explanation as to what the ♥♥♥ you just witnessed and learn more about things you have no reason (and/or no longer have reason) to care about. Lmao no - I rushed the final boss because I was that out of ♥♥♥ to give. E33 was so focused on painting a plot twist that it didn't care whether or not what it painted made sense. The start of act 2 and onwards feels like it was taken from a separate game idea and inserted clumsily into this one, with no regard given to whether or not it'd fit with the rest of the game, and all regard given to how unlikely it'd be for someone to guess the plot twist(s), which is obviously stupid writing that is doomed to sabotage any story and E33 is no exception. Given the previous points, my capacity to care about the rest of the story was already getting low, but I pressed onward hoping I'd see that life-changing masterpiece everyone talked about on the 25th hour or so only to run into act 2's finale and the game's ending(s) and encounter two middle fingers from the story as my reward. I wish my $40 a happy Gommage. Act 2's finale punishes you for caring, and so do the endings, both of which are bad, but one of which is "moral"/"good" by the game's standards. That ending finishes what act 2's finale starts. To continue my "set table" analogy at risk of spoilers: It lights the upended table on fire because you were too attached to it and it wasn't a "real" table anyway. The other ending is resetting the table but putting mannequins in all the seats. Both defeat the purpose of having a table. With how often you hear "for those who come after" in act 1, you'd think the story would continue that theme, but nope, it just shreds that in favor of a dumb plot twist that makes it ring hollow. The messages of the final act should flow well with the messages of the first but they're conveyed in the form of such convoluted twists that it feels more like the final act overwrites the first and doesn't pay off the story's hooks in a satisfying manner, destroying all intrigue, and rendering previous stakes and tension pointless. And that is the most I can say spoiler-free. Everything else about the game is so well-presented, but the story and some of the dialogue are the exact opposite. I guess you could say that's a very "Clair Obscur" contrast.

I used to play games to relax. I thought to myself, "Man, modern gaming is too sweaty. I just want a nice, colorful co-op adventure where my friends and I can chill, enjoy nature, and look at some cool low-poly scenery." Then I booted up PEAK and realized it is actually a psychological horror game disguised as a cute scouting trip. Now, three hours later, I am dangling by a single pixel off a sheer cliff face. My entire life depends on my buddy, who is currently hyperventilating into his mic because his hand is slipping on his desk. "HOLD ME," I’m screeching, watching the literal lava at the bottom of image_69df55.png mock our existence. One tiny, microscopic slip of the mouse—one minor physics jank—and we are both plummeting 40 minutes of vertical progress straight back to the lobby. I haven't blinked in ten minutes. My hand is actively cramping from gripping my mouse like my actual life depends on it. I came here for a "co-op physics adventure," but my heart rate is higher than it’s ever been in my life. We started the session as a tightly-knit squad; we are ending it as bitter enemies who can't even agree on which rock to grab next. Verdict: 10/10. It will completely destroy your trust in human nature and test your grip strength to its absolute limits, but reaching that next checkpoint feels like conquering the world.

There are already many negative reviews that give very valuable feedback on the game. For whatever reason, it does not seem that anything is done to directly address issues raised by the playerbase. Rather, the devs have dealt with them peripherally, or just straight up insulted the playerbase with collaborations nobody asked for when technical issues are the most salient. There is nothing wrong with introducing new content, and it can be good when the game works. But the game barely works for most. Furthermore, its gameplay is decent, but highly overrated. There are many glaring issues with it: - The wounds mechanic. Some weapons rely more on the wounds mechanic to be effective. The wounds mechanic works in a "zero-sum" manner. Meaning that if one person takes the wound, everyone else in the session is deprived of it. So, for example, if you are a charged blade user and you're paired with bow users, good luck trying to activate savage axe mode. And when you can do so, you would have done so with great anxiety and at a cost to proper strategy and timing. There are other things to say about the wounds mechanic, such as the insane stunlock on monsters. - The maps are picturesque, visually stunning, but lacking in substance and/or complexity. On this note it is important to compare it with Monster Hunter World (it's predecessor). The maps in Monster Hunter World may not have been as big, but there was more "content" packed into its area compared to the ones in Wilds. For whatever jank it had, MHWorld had more complex maps, and interactions with the environment that seemed more organic- not just pretty but flat maps with theatrical QTEs. So the end result is you have spaces that look good but feel hollow. - The weapons don't feel great anymore. So many weapons have glaring issues, and those who main each respective one will tell you exactly what is wrong with them. Many changes to the weapons from previous titles don't make any sense on the whole. I myself stopped using the charged blade entirely in MHWilds, which was my favourite weapon in MHWorld. This is not to say that no improvements could have been made to the weapons in MHWorld, but the way they approached it in MHWilds seems to lack careful evaluation of feedback provided by fans of MHWorld and MHRise. The crux of the matter is, in their effort to streamline and "improve" the accessibility of the game, many weapons have a more fixed way of being played, or have simply been dumbed down in general. Some changes to the weapons render certain moves pointless altogether. MHWilds had every opportunity to take from and improve systems from its predecessors (MHWorld and MHRise). MHRise for example allowed Hunters to customise weapon movesets, which introduced different ways to use the weapon and adds more satisfaction because of the variety and added flavour. You would think MHWilds would adapt something similar to this, considering its much bigger scope, budget, prior material, and scale, right? Nope. After all those years of development, and the insane starting price of the base game, this is how they justify it. Nothing really new or innovative has been added to the mix. No real substantial additions. No new weapons. No new ground-breaking fun ways to use already existing weapons. - Difficulty and accessibility. The Monster Hunter series has always featured the balance between preparation and execution. MHWilds undermines this balance by becoming the most forgiving entry in the series. There is often little consequence to mistakes, paired with overpowered blocking and the heavy emphasis on perfect blocks. The point of Monster Hunter was never about artificial difficulty, but rewarding mastery and deliberate play. In MHWilds, that diluted sense of mastery, alongside the overly-simplified weapon systems and rigid playstyles, makes combat feel flat and less engaging. - Loss of tension and identity. As an extension of the previous point, MHWilds lacks a genuine sense of danger- something that heavily characterises all its previous titles. Previous titles excelled at making monsters feel intimidating and memorable. First encounters with monsters like Nergigante, Bazelgeuse, etc. were tense and overwhelming. Monsters commanded more respect with their presence. But MHWilds rarely achieves this. Encounters with monsters feel a lot more choreographed and less threatening. What comes from this is a game that has monsters with superficial spectacle, but no real threat substantiating it. Aside from problems with gameplay (and I'm sure I've also missed out on many other important ones), other issues abound: - Technical issues. Ironically, while the game attempts to become "accessible" to players by dumbing down mechanical depth and punishment, it becomes less accessible in practice due to its technical state. MHWilds places extremely heavy demands on hardware, effectively locking out many players (and long-time fans) who use systems that don't cost you a kidney. In contrast, other modern titles (such as the free game Where Winds Meet) has both smooth gameplay and very decent graphics without requiring top-end GPUs. - The story. The Monster Hunter series was never known for having the most compelling stories, but again, with all the resources they had, whatever you see in the game is an absolute joke. For the record, there are games that cost a lot cheaper, with much smaller teams, that have way more compelling stories. Even a free game like the new Where Winds Meet has a story so much more compelling. - Monetisation. For reference, the starting price of the base game is already extremely high. It was 70 USD, 60 GBP, 100 SGD, etc. And yet there are still features you would expect to not cost anything additional... that cost additional. For example, the game charges you real money each time you edit your character after the first time you do so. There's also a sneaking suspicion that they would intentionally make "free" gear/layered armour unattractive, just to compel players to spend real money on cosmetics. - Messaging. Referring to updates as "Free Title Updates" is extremely disingenuous, as it frames essential fixes and late-arriving features as "bonuses" rather than necessary completions of an unfinished product. This ranges from technical to content issues (or the lack of content altogether). After almost 10 months, its players are getting late-delivered fixes (which haven't really worked at this point in time) for an extremely high-priced game that really needed more time to cook, and they market it as exciting content drops. Furthermore, capcom's fiscal year ended on 31 March 2025, while MHWilds launched on 28 February 2025. This timing allowed Capcom to record roughly 10 million unit sales in its final report. Coupled with the technical state at launch, and its severe lack of content, it would be reasonable to infer that Capcom prioritised corporate goals at the cost of severely undermining the quality of MHWilds. Gamers/Hunters lost, and the shareholders won. In July, Capcom also issued a formal policy warning that it would take legal action and pursue criminal proceedings against customers whose feedback exceeded "socially accepted standards". Capcom is happy to take premium prices for an unfinished product, but considers it a breach of social standards when the fans who funded that success express dissatisfaction with the result. (See also RainbowKrampus’ 12 December review for a critique of MHWilds’ PC performance) Regardless of whether the issues ultimately stem from the developers or the corporate leadership, the end result is that players were charged a premium price for a product that was neither finished nor honestly presented at launch. This conduct is predatory and exploitative. What is most disappointing, however, is not merely the presence of technical or design flaws. Capcom eroded trust- trust that was built over years and then severely undermined with this release cycle.
